Put $B=K_0^{-1}V$. The coefficient of $z^n$ in
$S=\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^nK_0^{-1}$ is finite. In
$(I+zB)\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n$, the constant coefficient is $I$ and the two
terms in every positive degree cancel. Since $K=K_0(I+zB)$, this proves
$KS=I$. The same coefficient cancellation in
$\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n(I+zB)$ proves $SK=I$. At $z=0$ this reduces to
$S(0)=K_0^{-1}$.

For the first current, $\not k=\not p-\not p'$, so the right equation

$k_aJ_1^a=\bar u(p')(\not p-\not p')u(p)
=\mu\bar u(p')u(p)-\mu\bar u(p')u(p)=0$. For the second current its transfer
is $q-q'=-k$; the same calculation gives $(-k)_bJ_2^b=0$, hence

The hypotheses match [L1]'s finite formal matrix interface. Replacing

coefficient of $S$ by $D_\theta$, because
$(D_\theta K_0D_\theta^{-1})^{-1}=D_\theta K_0^{-1}D_\theta^{-1}$ and
matrix products associate. Hence $S(z;\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta
S(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}$. With $K_s=K(z;\zeta^{s\theta})$, $S_s=S(z;\zeta^{s\theta})$ and $\delta$ as defined in the Statement, differentiating $K_sS_s=I$ coefficientwise at $s=0$ gives
$\delta S=-S(\delta K)S$; differentiating $D_s=e^{is\Theta}$ gives
$\delta K=i[\Theta,K]$, and substitution with $KS=SK=I$ yields

By step 2.1 and [F5],
$\det K(z;\zeta^\theta)=\det(D_\theta K(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1})
=\det(D_\theta)\det(K(z;\zeta))\det(D_\theta^{-1})$.
The finite matrices $D_\theta$ and $D_\theta^{-1}$ are inverse, so [F5]

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings

Adopt the following specified free-photon model in the oriented,
time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and length coordinates of
[[def-qft-framework-units]], with metric $(-,+,+,+)$ and $x^0=ct$. The
classical electromagnetic input is the smooth source-free branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]; the electromagnetic two-form and its potential
components are those of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and a supplied
potential is subject to [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. These EM suppliers
are physical input and conventions: they do not by themselves construct a
quantum representation.

For almost every $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, set
$\mathbf n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}$. The mathematical
definition [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]] specifies the positive
one-photon Hilbert space

$$\mathcal H_T= \{u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3): \mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\},$$

with the inherited pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k$,
linear in the second variable as in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The
value assigned to $P_T$ at
$\mathbf k=0$ is immaterial because that point has Lebesgue measure zero; no
continuous polarization frame over all momentum directions is chosen. Adopt
the bosonic Fock representation $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ and the free
Hamiltonian

$$H_\gamma=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|),$$

where on the $n$-photon sector $d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$ is multiplication by
$\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ and is zero on the vacuum sector. Its exact
self-adjoint domain and the unitary mass-cone action are those in the
mathematical supplier [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]]. The actual
smeared field-strength distributions and bounded Weyl operators are those
constructed in [[lem-qft-photon-local-weyl-observables]]; a pointwise
potential or field-strength operator is not asserted to exist. These
mathematical suppliers are draft carriers with mixed current Step 1 status: the
transverse-space, null-quotient, covariance-spectrum, framework-units, and
C01 measurement carriers have current ready records; the local-Weyl carrier is
escalated through its field-strength prerequisite. Readiness records are not
independent approval, and every use remains conditional on the exact statement
and proof supplied.

For the physical interpretation of an actually constructed state and a
supplied normalized measurement instrument, use
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]: Born probabilities are
assigned only to that specified model and instrument. This postulate records
the model's free Maxwell quanta as photons. It does not assert that the
model has been empirically confirmed, and it introduces no interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, LSZ limit,
asymptotic completeness, or nonperturbative continuum limit. In calculations
using an indefinite four-polarization auxiliary space, only the positive
transverse model or its separately constructed null quotient is physical;
four auxiliary components are not four positive photon states.

Assume Countable Choice. On the future null cone write $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$, $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, $\mathbf k\ne0$, and use the measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. The fiber $p^\perp/\mathbb Cp$ has the positive quotient form of [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]. For each proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$, the action
$$[s(p)]\longmapsto[\Lambda s(\Lambda^{-1}p)]$$
is a unitary representation on the square-integrable quotient sections. It is strongly continuous. Under the unitary identification with $\mathcal H_T$ given by
$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Its bosonic Fock lift has joint spectrum the closed future cone
$$\overline V_+=\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\},$$
with the vacuum at $(0,\mathbf0)$. The energy is the nonnegative sector multiplier $\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ with the exact maximal square-integrability domain on each sector and square-summability over sectors. These are mathematical free-field representation statements.

Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

derivations.claim:
For $\mathbf n\in S^2$, set
$b(\mathbf n)=\lambda(I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T)\mathbf e$. Then
$\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$. Since $\mathbf e$ is unit,
$|b(\mathbf n)|^2=\lambda^2(1-(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e)^2)$. The function
is continuous on $S^2$ and hence measurable.

By the orthogonal invariance in [F4], take $\mathbf e$ as the third coordinate axis and put $u=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e$. The chart $X(u,\phi)=(\sqrt{1-u^2}\cos\phi,\sqrt{1-u^2}\sin\phi,u)$ for $-1<u<1$, $0<\phi<2\pi$ has orthogonal tangent vectors with squared lengths $(1-u^2)^{-1}$ and $1-u^2$, so [F5] gives area density $1$. The omitted seam is a coordinate line in sphere graph charts and the poles are singletons; [F7] makes their chart integrals zero. Thus spherical integration gives
$$C_b=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2d\Omega =2\pi\lambda^2\int_{-1}^1(1-u^2)\,du =\frac{8\pi\lambda^2}{3}>0.$$
Using $d^3\mathbf k=r^2dr\,d\Omega$ and
$|f_\epsilon(r\mathbf n)|^2=r^{-3}|b(\mathbf n)|^2$ gives
$$\|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\int_\epsilon^\kappa\frac{dr}{r} =C_b\log(\kappa/\epsilon),\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}\hbar c|\mathbf k||f_\epsilon(\mathbf k)|^2d^3\mathbf k =\hbar c C_b\int_\epsilon^\kappa dr =\hbar c C_b(\kappa-\epsilon).$$
Both integrals are finite because $0<\epsilon<\kappa$. The profile has units
$\mathrm m^{3/2}$ because $|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}$ has those units and $b$ is
dimensionless; the energy integral has units joules because $\hbar c$ has
units joule-metres. Thus $b$ satisfies the nonzero transverse-profile
hypothesis of [L2] with the conventions [F1].

The definition of $b$ gives
$f_\epsilon(\mathbf k)=\mathbf1_{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa}
|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b(\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|)$. Applying [L2] with
$C_b=8\pi\lambda^2/3$ and the Hamiltonian of [L1] gives the normalized
coherent vector, its energy domain membership, both expectation
formulas, weak convergence to zero, and failure of strong Fock-space
convergence. For the number domain, put $r=\|f_\epsilon\|^2$. By [F3],
its squared sector norms are $e^{-r}r^n/n!$, so reindexing the absolutely
convergent exponential series gives
$\sum_{n\ge1}n^2e^{-r}r^n/n!=r^2+r<\infty$. The maximal number
multiplier from [F6] therefore contains this vector in its domain. This
restriction to the transverse space preserves the domain because each
sector multiplier $nI$ preserves every transverse symmetric sector. The item-level suppliers are present in the active manifests,
but [L1] has no Step-1 record and [L2] is escalated, so this application
remains conditional rather than accepted.

Let $\epsilon_j=\kappa 2^{-j}$ for $j\ge1$. By step 3.1 the difference
$f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}$ is supported on
$\epsilon_{j+1}<|\mathbf k|<\epsilon_j$, so spherical integration gives
$$\|f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}\|^2 =C_b\int_{\epsilon_{j+1}}^{\epsilon_j}\frac{dr}{r} =C_b\log 2>0.$$
From the Fock direct-sum pairing in [F3], the tensor product pairing on
sector $n$ gives
$$\langle C(f),C(g)\rangle =e^{-(\|f\|^2+\|g\|^2)/2} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\langle f,g\rangle^n}{n!} =e^{-(\|f\|^2+\|g\|^2)/2+\langle f,g\rangle},$$
where the series is absolutely convergent by
$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|\|g\|$. Hence
 $|\langle C(f),C(g)\rangle|=e^{-\|f-g\|^2/2}$. By [L2],
$\|C(f_{\epsilon_j})\|=1$ for each $j$. For any choices of phases
$\alpha_j\in\mathbb R$, the unit vectors
$v_j=e^{i\alpha_j}C(f_{\epsilon_j})$ satisfy
$$\|v_{j+1}-v_j\|^2 =2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle v_j,v_{j+1}\rangle \ge2(1-e^{-C_b\log 2/2})>0.$$
This bound holds for every phase sequence, so none is Cauchy. Any
phase-adjusted norm limit as $\epsilon\downarrow0$ would restrict to a
Cauchy sequence along $\epsilon_j$; therefore no such limit exists.

By [L2], each vector has norm one and the weak limit is zero. Since the
zero vector has norm zero, it is not a normalized state; the nonexistence of
a norm limit follows from steps 3.1 and 4.1.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim:
For each $\mathbf k\ne0$, $n^Tn=n\cdot n=1$ by [F2], so $P_T^*=P_T$ and
$$P_T^2=(I-nn^T)^2=I-2nn^T+n(n^Tn)n^T=I-nn^T=P_T.$$
Its complex kernel is $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{n\}$ and its
range is the Hermitian perpendicular plane $n^\perp$, of complex dimension
two. For $z\in\mathbb C^3$, put $a=n^Tz$. The specified Hermitian pairing
and realness of $n$ give
$\|P_Tz\|^2=\sum_j|z_j-n_ja|^2=\|z\|^2-|a|^2\le\|z\|^2$.
Thus it is contractive, with norm one because it fixes every unit vector in
that nonzero perpendicular plane. The arbitrary value at the single point $\mathbf k=0$ does not affect its multiplication operator on $L^2$.

Under [A2], [A1] makes each complex scalar $L^2$ component complete for its first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=\int u\overline v$. The three-component direct sum is complete componentwise. Its second-variable-linear pairing is $\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1=\int\overline u\cdot v$, with the same norm; [F1] fixes this convention. Thus $\mathcal H$ is complete. The multiplier $M_{P_T}$ is bounded and idempotent by step 1.1. If $u_r=M_{P_T}v_r\to u$ in $\mathcal H$, then $M_{P_T}u=\lim_rM_{P_T}u_r=\lim_ru_r=u$ by boundedness, so $u$ belongs to its range. Thus $\mathcal H_T$ is closed and inherits a positive Hilbert inner product. Since $P_Tu=u$ is equivalent to $n\cdot u=0$ for unit $n$ by [F2], the pointwise range formula gives the displayed transverse condition almost everywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

For every positive even integer $n$, no continuous map $v:S^n\to\mathbb R^{n+1}$ can satisfy both $\langle v(x),x\rangle=0$ and $v(x)\ne0$ for all $x$. Thus an even-dimensional sphere has no continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field.

derivations.claim: If such a frame existed, then $e_1(n)\in n^\perp$ for every $n$ by [F1], and $|e_1(n)|=1$ by orthonormality. Therefore $e_1$ is a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^2$.
Since $2$ is a positive even integer, [F2] forbids the vector field produced in step 1.1. This contradiction proves the nonexistence of the global frame.

boundaries.reason: Statement of No global continuous real polarization frame: Assume Countable Choice. For $n\in S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$, let $E_n=n^\perp=\operatorname{Ran}(I-nn^T)$ be the real transverse plane. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

Thus $\mathcal K_0=\ker Q$ is closed. For $\epsilon\in\mathcal K_0$, $n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=\epsilon^0$, so $n\cdot T\epsilon=0$ and $T\epsilon\in\mathcal H_T$ by [F1]. Also $\|T\epsilon\|_2\le\|\boldsymbol\epsilon\|_2+\|\epsilon^0\|_2$, proving boundedness.

Write $\boldsymbol\epsilon=T\epsilon+n\epsilon^0$ and $\boldsymbol\delta=T\delta+n\delta^0$. Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for

bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$

[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.

second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;

the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let

[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and

$n$-particle sectors.

$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.

$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where

creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the

$$\phi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathbf A\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R^3),\qquad \psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4),\qquad \chi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R).$$

Then $F_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ has smooth real component maps $F_{ab}:U\to\mathbb R$. The spinor is an ordinary commuting $\mathbb C^4$-valued map, not a tuple of Grassmann generators. Its Dirac adjoint is the smooth row-valued map $\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta:U\to(\mathbb C^4)^*$, using the fixed matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], so $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$. For periodic spatial domains, the same component and unit conventions apply to smooth periodic coordinate lifts, with the quotient domain specified by the item using them.

In the current SI, $c$ and $h$ are defining constants while $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined; the formula below keeps $\mu_0$ symbolic and assigns it no numerical value. Use the lower-potential convention
$$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),$$

$$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c},\qquad a_a=A_a/S_0,\qquad f_{ab}=\partial_aa_b-\partial_ba_a,$$

For the real smooth gauge-parameter map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R$ in webers, put $\alpha:=\chi/S_0\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ (dimensionless) and use

The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

Fix $\mu\ge0$, $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$, and the Dirac matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]; $\mu$ is the inverse-length mathematical shell parameter of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. $$\delta S_\phi(\phi;h)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h(\Box-\mu^2)\phi\,d^4x,\qquad \delta S_D(\psi;\chi)=2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R^4}\chi^\dagger\beta\left(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu\right)\psi\,d^4x.$$

The adjoint Dirac equation follows from the second equation because the fixed matrices satisfy $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$. These are mathematical variation identities for commuting classical fields; they assert no quantization, Grassmann calculus, or physical measurement.

derivations.claim: Under $a\mapsto a+\partial\alpha$ and $\psi\mapsto e^{ig\alpha}\psi$, the chain rule gives $D'_a\psi'=e^{ig\alpha}D_a\psi$; the conjugate equation gives $D'_a\bar\psi'=e^{-ig\alpha}D_a\bar\psi$. The two phases cancel in each term of $\mathcal L_D$, so the density is gauge invariant. The explicit Countable Choice assumption is [A2].

From [F2], $\beta=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2)$ is Hermitian and squares to $I_4$; each Pauli matrix is Hermitian, so $\alpha_j^\dagger=\alpha_j$, and the block formulas give $\alpha_j\beta=-\beta\alpha_j$. Therefore $(\gamma^0)^\dagger\beta=\beta^2=I_4=\beta\gamma^0$, while for $j=1,2,3$,
$$ (\gamma^j)^\dagger\beta=(\beta\alpha_j)^\dagger\beta=\alpha_j\beta^\dagger\beta=\alpha_j=\beta^2\alpha_j=\beta\gamma^j. $$
This proves [F3] from the exact matrix definitions. Now vary $\psi$ along a compactly supported complex $\chi$ and $\bar\psi$ along $\bar\chi$. Expanding the four kinetic terms and integrating the terms containing $D_a\chi$ or $D_a\bar\chi$ by parts gives
$$\delta S_D=2\operatorname{Re}\int_U\chi^\dagger\beta R_D\,d^4x, \qquad R_D=(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi.$$
For example, $\int\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\chi=-\int(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\chi$ and $-\int(D_a\bar\chi)\gamma^a\psi=\int\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi$; compact support removes both boundary terms. The resulting variation is
$$i\int\bigl(\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi-(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\chi\bigr)d^4x-\mu\int(\bar\chi\psi+\bar\psi\chi)d^4x =\int\bigl(\bar\chi R_D+\overline{\bar\chi R_D}\bigr)d^4x,$$
where the equality uses $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$ from [F3]. If $R_D(x_0)\ne0$, continuity and openness of $U$ give a ball contained in $U$ where $|R_D|>0$; choose a bump $\rho$ from [F4] there and take $\chi=\rho\beta R_D$. Since $\beta^\dagger\beta=I_4$, this gives $\delta S_D=2\int\rho|R_D|^2d^4x>0$, contradicting stationarity. Thus stationarity is equivalent to $R_D=0$ pointwise, and taking the adjoint gives $-i(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi=0$. This is the charged version of the compact-variation identity in [F1]; the additional $a_a$ terms are smooth multiplication terms.

Contract the first equation in step 1.2 on the left by $\bar\psi$ and the adjoint equation on the right by $\psi$. Subtracting cancels the equal mass terms and gives
$$i\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi+(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)=0.$$
The parenthesis equals $\partial_a(\bar\psi\gamma^a\psi)$ because the $+ig a_a\bar\psi$ and $-ig a_a\psi$ contributions cancel. Since $i\ne0$ and $g$ is constant, $\partial_a j^a=0$.

From [A1], $g/S_0=q/\hbar$, so $ga_j=qA_j/\hbar$ and $ga_0=-q\phi/(\hbar c)$; also $x^0=ct$ and $\mu=mc/\hbar$. With $\gamma^0=\beta$ and $\gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j$ [F2], multiply the equation in step 1.2 by $\beta$ and then by $\hbar c$. Collecting the time derivative gives
$$i\hbar\partial_t\psi=\left[c\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot(-i\hbar\nabla-q\mathbf A)+\beta mc^2+q\phi\right]\psi.$$
This verifies the stated minimal-coupling signs.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

Fix an inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] and identify its vector coordinates with $\mathbb R^4$ and $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi\in\mathbb R$, define the boost $B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)$ by $B e_0=\cosh\chi\,e_0+\sinh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, $B\mathbf n_B=\sinh\chi\,e_0+\cosh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, and $Bw=w$ for every $w$ Euclidean-orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n_B)$. Every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]], admits $\Lambda=B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$, where $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ fixes the time axis and $\mathbf n_R$, and sends $\mathbf v_\perp$ to $\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n_R\times\mathbf v_\perp$ on the orthogonal plane, where $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$; the cross product is [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. If $\Lambda e_0=e_0$, choose $\chi=0$ and $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)=\Lambda$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

By [F5], $\Lambda$ preserves $\eta$ and sends a future null vector $p$ to a future null vector $\Lambda p$. It maps $p^\perp$ onto $(\Lambda p)^\perp$ and $\mathbb Cp$ onto $\mathbb C\Lambda p$, so it induces a well-defined map on the quotient fiber. The induced form is preserved because $\eta(\Lambda v,\Lambda w)=\eta(v,w)$; hence the fiber map is an isometry. The map $T_p$ is independent of the representative: replacing
$\epsilon$ by $\epsilon+cp$ changes its value by
$c(\mathbf k-(\mathbf k/\omega)\omega)=0$.
For $\epsilon\in p^\perp$, $\mathbf k\cdot T_p[\epsilon]=0$;
its pairing is the positive quotient pairing of [F1]. The lift
$\epsilon=(0,\sqrt{2\omega}\,u(\mathbf k))$ for transverse $u$ proves
surjectivity, and $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$ gives
$\int\|T_p[s(p)]\|^2d\nu=\int\|u(\mathbf k)\|^2d^3\mathbf k$.
Thus the stated section identification is well-defined and unitary.
Applying two Lorentz maps successively gives the representation composition law.

For the boost $B_n(\chi)$ in [F2], put $\beta=\tanh\chi$ and $\gamma=\cosh\chi$, so $|\beta|<1$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$. In Euclidean unit direction $n$ [F5], its spatial cone coordinates satisfy
$$\mathbf k'=\mathbf k+(\gamma-1)(n\cdot\mathbf k)n-\gamma\beta\omega n,\qquad \omega'=\gamma(\omega-\beta n\cdot\mathbf k).$$
Taking $n$ as the third coordinate axis, the first two spatial coordinates are unchanged and
$$\frac{\partial k'_3}{\partial k_3} =\gamma\left(1-\beta\frac{k_3}{\omega}\right)=\frac{\omega'}{\omega}.$$
Thus $\det(\partial\mathbf k'/\partial\mathbf k)=\omega'/\omega$. A rotation has determinant one and preserves $\omega$. By [F2], every proper orthochronous $\Lambda$ is a product of these, so $d^3\mathbf k'/(2\omega')=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. Combining this change of variables with the fiber isometry in step 1.1 proves unitarity on the quotient-section space and verifies the stated identification with $\mathcal H_T$.

For $v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, consider the bundle section $s_v(p)=\sqrt{2\omega}\,P_T(\mathbf k)v(\mathbf k)$; under the stated unitary identification it corresponds exactly to $u=P_Tv\in\mathcal H_T$. In the transverse chart the transformed section is $T_p(\Lambda s_v(\Lambda^{-1}p))$, where $T_p$ is the explicit continuous fiber quotient map of [F1]. Its support stays in a fixed compact set for Lorentz transformations near the identity. Away from an arbitrarily small ball about $\mathbf k=0$, the momentum maps and fiber maps vary uniformly continuously; inside that ball $s_v$ is bounded and the $d\nu$ measure tends to zero with the radius. Hence the transformed sections converge in $L^2(d\nu)$ as $\Lambda\to I$. Such sections are dense: approximate any $u\in\mathcal H_T$ by $v\in C_c^\infty$ using [F4], and apply the bounded projection $P_T$; the transformed maps are unitary by step 2.1, so density extends continuity to every section. The Fock lift is strongly continuous on finite tensor products and the vacuum by this one-particle continuity; finite-particle vectors are dense, and its unitary bound extends continuity to all Fock space.

The measure for the one-particle shell is sigma-finite by [F6]. The phase in the statement is multiplication by the four-vector $(\omega,-\mathbf k)$. Identify $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with scalar $L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\{1,2,3\})$ using counting measure on the three labels; [F3] then gives the joint PVM with sector multipliers $(\sum_r|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_r\mathbf k_r)$ and their exact maximal domains. On each one-particle sector $P_T(\mathbf k)$ commutes with every scalar multiplier $1_B(|\mathbf k|,-\mathbf k)$; hence $P_T^{\otimes n}$ commutes with the n-particle joint PVM and multiplier. The symmetric transverse sector is reducing, so restriction preserves the exact multiplier domain. Each joint value $(\sum_r|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_r\mathbf k_r)$ lies in $\overline V_+$ by the triangle inequality. Conversely, every nonzero lightlike boundary point is in the support of the one-particle measure, since every neighborhood of its momentum has positive measure and a nonzero transverse fiber. For $E>|\mathbf P|$, choose $\mathbf k_1=-\mathbf P/2+q n$ and $\mathbf k_2=-\mathbf P/2-q n$ with $n\perp\mathbf P$ and $q=\tfrac12\sqrt{E^2-|\mathbf P|^2}$ (when $\mathbf P=0$, choose any unit $n$). Then $|\mathbf k_1|+|\mathbf k_2|=E$ and $-(\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2)=\mathbf P$. Small neighborhoods of these nonzero momenta have positive measure and nonzero transverse fibers, so every neighborhood of $(E,\mathbf P)$ has nonzero two-particle spectral projection. The vacuum supplies the origin. Thus the joint spectrum is exactly $\overline V_+$, and [F3] gives the exact energy domain.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $j=(j_1,j_2,j_3)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ and use $\mathcal H_T$ and $P_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. For $\omega=|\mathbf k|$ and $\mathbf k\ne0$, define
$$g_j(\mathbf k)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}}\, P_T(\mathbf k)\int_{\mathbb R^4}j(x)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^4x.$$
Then $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$. On the finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$, the smeared transverse potential is
$$A_T(j)=a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j).$$
Its matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology; it is an operator-valued distribution and does not assign a pointwise operator to $A_i(x)$. With $E_i=-\partial_0A_i$, the equal-time canonical commutator is the distribution
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)] =-i\,P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. On the future null cone write $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$, $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, $\mathbf k\ne0$, and use the measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. The fiber $p^\perp/\mathbb Cp$ has the positive quotient form of [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]. For each proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$, the action
$$[s(p)]\longmapsto[\Lambda s(\Lambda^{-1}p)]$$
is a unitary representation on the square-integrable quotient sections. It is strongly continuous. Under the unitary identification with $\mathcal H_T$ given by
$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Its bosonic Fock lift has joint spectrum the closed future cone
$$\overline V_+=\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\},$$
with the vacuum at $(0,\mathbf0)$. The energy is the nonnegative sector multiplier $\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ with the exact maximal square-integrability domain on each sector and square-summability over sectors. These are mathematical free-field representation statements.

Assume Countable Choice. For $\mu\ge0$, define the tempered distribution
$$\Delta_\mu(t,\mathbf x)= \int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3} \frac{\sin(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)t)}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)} e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x},$$
with the massless integrand defined off $\mathbf k=0$; its $1/|\mathbf k|$
behavior is locally integrable in three dimensions. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\Delta_\mu \subseteq\{(t,\mathbf x):t^2-|\mathbf x|^2\ge0\},$$
the closed causal cone for the $(-+++)$ metric. For real compactly supported
smooth $f,g$, put
$$\Delta_\mu(f,g)= \int_{\mathbb R^4}\!\int_{\mathbb R^4} f(x)g(y)\Delta_\mu(x-y)\,d^4x\,d^4y.$$
On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the smeared fields of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] satisfy
$$[\Phi_\mu(f),\Phi_\mu(g)]=-i\Delta_\mu(f,g)I.$$
Consequently spacelike-separated supports give commuting fields.

derivations.claim:
Antisymmetry gives
$$\frac12\int(\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a)h^{ab}\,d^4x =\int\partial_aA_b\,h^{ab}\,d^4x =-\int A_b\,\partial_a h^{ab}\,d^4x,$$
where integration by parts has no boundary term because $h$ is compactly supported. The current $j^b=-\partial_a h^{ab}$ obeys $\partial_bj^b=-\partial_b\partial_a h^{ab}=0$, since exchanging $a,b$ changes the sign of $h$. Adding $\partial_b\lambda$ to $A_b$ changes the last integral by $\int\lambda\,\partial_b\partial_a h^{ab}=0$. The spatial components of $j$ are compact smooth, so [F1] supplies the vector $g_h=g_j$ and the stated finite-particle operator.

A null-cone polarization representative $\epsilon_b$ contributes to a field-strength coefficient through $p_a\epsilon_b-p_b\epsilon_a$. Replacing $\epsilon$ by $\epsilon+c p$ leaves this expression unchanged because $p_ap_b-p_bp_a=0$. Under a Lorentz transformation both $p$ and $\epsilon$ transform linearly, so their antisymmetric product transforms as a two-form. The unitary quotient action [F2] therefore intertwines the smeared tensor test with its Lorentz pullback, proving covariance without choosing a global polarization frame.

The mode formula in [F1] and the CCR give, after changing $\mathbf k$ to $-\mathbf k$ in the negative-frequency term,
$$[A_i(x),A_j(y)]=\left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{k_i k_j}{|\mathbf k|^2}\right)C_0(x-y)$$
as the spatial Fourier multiplier distribution. Differentiating, using $\partial_{x^0}\partial_{y^0}=-\partial_0^2$, gives $[E_i,E_j]=-\partial_0^2P_{T,ij}C_0$. The massless equation $\partial_0^2C_0=\Delta C_0$ follows by differentiating the sine-over-$|\mathbf k|$ integral in [F3]. The multiplier of $-\Delta P_{T,ij}$ is $\delta_{ij}|\mathbf k|^2-k_ik_j$, which is exactly the multiplier of $-\delta_{ij}\Delta+\partial_i\partial_j$; this proves the stated electric commutator. For magnetic fields, each curl kills the longitudinal multiplier $k_sk_u/|\mathbf k|^2$, and $\epsilon_{irs}\epsilon_{jts}k_rk_t=\delta_{ij}|\mathbf k|^2-k_ik_j$ gives the same expression. For the mixed commutator, translation invariance gives $\partial_{y^r}=-\partial_{x^r}$, so
$$[E_i(x),B_j(y)]=\epsilon_{jrs}\partial_0\partial_rP_{T,is}C_0.$$
The longitudinal term is zero because $\epsilon_{jrs}k_rk_s=0$, and relabeling the remaining indices gives $\epsilon_{jri}\partial_0\partial_rC_0$.

If a test function is supported in the complement of $\operatorname{supp}C_0$, each of its derivatives has support contained in that of the test function, and the definition $\langle\partial_a C_0,f\rangle=-\langle C_0,\partial_af\rangle$ shows the derivative distribution also vanishes there. Thus every derivative in step 2.2 remains supported in the closed causal cone from [F3]. For spacelike-separated compact test supports, every point in their difference set lies outside that cone, so pairing each commutator with their tensor product gives zero. The smeared field strengths commute on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Work in the fixed length coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf w$; write $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$. For subsets $S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, say they are **spacelike separated** when $\eta(x-y,x-y)=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2-(x^0-y^0)^2>0$ for every $x\in S$ and $y\in T$. Let $A_0=0$ and let $A_i$ be the transverse potential operator-valued distribution of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]]. Set
$$F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,\qquad E_i=-\partial_0A_i,\qquad B_i=\epsilon_{irs}\partial_rA_s,$$
where $\epsilon_{irs}$ is the totally antisymmetric symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$. In the commutator formulas below, $\Delta=\sum_{r=1}^3\partial_r^2$ is the spatial Laplacian acting on $x-y$.
For a real antisymmetric test tensor $h=(h^{ab})$ with $h^{ab}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)$ and $h^{ab}=-h^{ba}$, define
$$F(h)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}F_{ab}(x)h^{ab}(x)\,d^4x =-A_b(\partial_a h^{ab}).$$
The effective test is conserved, $\partial_b\partial_a h^{ab}=0$, and $F(h)$ is unchanged by $A_b\mapsto A_b+\partial_b\lambda$ for smooth $\lambda$. Its one-particle coefficient $g_h$ is the vector $g_j$ of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]] for $j_i=-\partial_a h^{ai}$, so $F(h)=a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h)$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

Let $C_0=-i\Delta_0$, where $\Delta_0$ is the massless scalar causal commutator of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. As distributions in $x-y$,
$$[E_i(x),E_j(y)]=[B_i(x),B_j(y)] =(-\delta_{ij}\Delta+\partial_i\partial_j)C_0(x-y),$$
$$[E_i(x),B_j(y)]=\epsilon_{jri}\partial_0\partial_rC_0(x-y).$$
Every right-hand side has support in the closed causal cone. Hence compactly supported tests whose supports are spacelike separated in the stated Minkowski sense give commuting field-strength operators on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The quotient representation of [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]] makes these smeared field strengths Lorentz covariant: their on-shell coefficient depends on a polarization class only through $p_a\epsilon_b-p_b\epsilon_a$. These conclusions concern gauge-invariant free observables and do not assert locality of the Coulomb potential.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and let $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ be its bosonic Fock space and finite-particle domain.
For $h\in H$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the Segal field
$$\phi_0(h):=2^{-1/2}\bigl(a^\dagger(h)+a(h)\bigr).$$
For $h\ne0$, this symmetric operator is essentially self-adjoint; write
$\Phi(h)=\overline{\phi_0(h)}$. If $r=\|h\|$, $e=h/r$, $K=e^\perp$,
$G=\mathcal F_s(K)$, choose a countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $G$
whose vectors are finite-particle, and use the one-mode splitting of
[[lem-qft-fock-one-mode-splitting]] followed by the Hermite unitary
$|n\rangle\mapsto g_n$ into $L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ with pairing
$\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int\overline f g$ to write a vector as
$(f_j)_{j\in J}\in\ell^2(J;L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C))$. Then the exact domain and
action are
$$D(\Phi(h))=\left\{(f_j):\sum_{j\in J}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+r^2x^2)|f_j(x)|^2\,dx<\infty\right\},\qquad (\Phi(h)f)_j(x)=rx f_j(x).$$
For $h=0$, $\phi_0(0)$ closes to the zero operator on all of $\mathcal F_s(H)$.

Define $\epsilon(z)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}z^{\otimes n}/\sqrt{n!}$ for $z\in H$.
There are unitaries $W(h)$ determined on these total exponential vectors by
$$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$
They obey
$$W(h)W(k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{2}\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle_2\right)W(h+k),\qquad \langle\Omega,W(h)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|h\|^2/4},$$
and $h\mapsto W(h)$ is strongly continuous. For every $h$, the one-parameter
group $t\mapsto W(th)$ has norm derivative at zero exactly on
$D(\Phi(h))$, with derivative $i\Phi(h)$ (for $h=0$ this is the zero
generator). Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the
closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim
is included.

derivations.claim: Let $D$ be the real countable dense family in [F3]. Then $D+iD$ is countable and dense in complex scalar $L^2$, because the squared norm of a complex error is the sum of the squared real- and imaginary-part errors. Its finite triple product is countable and dense in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. If $(v_n)$ enumerates that dense set, boundedness of $P_T$ makes $(P_Tv_n)$ dense in $\operatorname{Ran}P_T=\mathcal H_T$: for $u=P_Tu$, any $v_n\to u$ implies $P_Tv_n\to u$. Thus the separability hypothesis of [F4] holds, and the Segal supplier gives a bounded unitary $W_{\rm Segal}(u)$ for every $u\in\mathcal H_T$.

From [F1]–[F2], on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$,
$$[F(h),F(k)]=[a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h),a(g_k)+a^\dagger(g_k)] =(\langle g_h,g_k\rangle_2-\langle g_k,g_h\rangle_2)I =2i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle g_h,g_k\rangle_2\,I.$$
For spacelike-separated supports the left side vanishes by [F1], hence $\operatorname{Im}\langle g_h,g_k\rangle_2=0$.

The supplier's one-parameter group generated by the closed Segal field gives $W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2g_h)$ with generator $\sqrt2\,\Phi(g_h)=\overline{a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h)}$, which is the closure of $F(h)$ from [F1]. Thus $W_O(h)$ is the bounded Weyl observable associated to this field strength. It is unitary, and its real and imaginary parts are bounded self-adjoint operators with norm at most one.

The Weyl relation [F4] gives
$$W_O(h)W_O(k)=e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle\sqrt2g_h,\sqrt2g_k\rangle_2/2}W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2g_h+\sqrt2g_k).$$
By step 2.1 the phase is one for spacelike-separated tests, so $W_O(h)$ and $W_O(k)$ commute. Products, adjoints, and norm limits preserve commutation; therefore the norm-closed algebras of two spacelike-separated regions commute. Since $W_{\rm Segal}(0)=I$, these algebras are unital.
