The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

Assume Countable Choice. For $n\in S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$, let $E_n=n^\perp=\operatorname{Ran}(I-nn^T)$ be the real transverse plane. There do not exist continuous maps $e_1,e_2:S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ such that, for every $n$, $(e_1(n),e_2(n))$ is an orthonormal basis of $E_n$. A continuous real orthonormal polarization frame would in particular give a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^2$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Locally in direction space one can choose two continuous orthonormal polarization vectors. There is no continuous real orthonormal polarization frame on all of $S^2$. In the Lorenz auxiliary construction, the four-component subsidiary space modulo its null radical is isometric to this same two-dimensional transverse fiber; four auxiliary components do not represent four positive physical polarizations. The reverse iff axis adds no separately stated converse hypothesis here; the recorded claim is the displayed construction, identity, implication or scope qualification, not a characterization by a new necessary-and-sufficient condition.

citations.quote:
Adopt the following specified free-photon model in the oriented,
time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and length coordinates of
[[def-qft-framework-units]], with metric $(-,+,+,+)$ and $x^0=ct$. The
classical electromagnetic input is the smooth source-free branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]; the electromagnetic two-form and its potential
components are those of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and a supplied
potential is subject to [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. These EM suppliers
are physical input and conventions: they do not by themselves construct a
quantum representation.

For almost every $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, set
$\mathbf n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}$. The mathematical
definition [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]] specifies the positive
one-photon Hilbert space

$$\mathcal H_T= \{u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3): \mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\},$$

with the inherited pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k$,
linear in the second variable as in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The
value assigned to $P_T$ at
$\mathbf k=0$ is immaterial because that point has Lebesgue measure zero; no
continuous polarization frame over all momentum directions is chosen. Adopt
the bosonic Fock representation $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ and the free
Hamiltonian

$$H_\gamma=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|),$$

where on the $n$-photon sector $d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$ is multiplication by
$\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ and is zero on the vacuum sector. Its exact
self-adjoint domain and the unitary mass-cone action are those in the
mathematical supplier [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]]. The actual
smeared field-strength distributions and bounded Weyl operators are those
constructed in [[lem-qft-photon-local-weyl-observables]]; a pointwise
potential or field-strength operator is not asserted to exist. These
mathematical suppliers are draft carriers with mixed current Step 1 status: the
transverse-space, null-quotient, covariance-spectrum, framework-units, and
C01 measurement carriers have current ready records; the local-Weyl carrier is
escalated through its field-strength prerequisite. Readiness records are not
independent approval, and every use remains conditional on the exact statement
and proof supplied.

For the physical interpretation of an actually constructed state and a
supplied normalized measurement instrument, use
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]: Born probabilities are
assigned only to that specified model and instrument. This postulate records
the model's free Maxwell quanta as photons. It does not assert that the
model has been empirically confirmed, and it introduces no interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, LSZ limit,
asymptotic completeness, or nonperturbative continuum limit. In calculations
using an indefinite four-polarization auxiliary space, only the positive
transverse model or its separately constructed null quotient is physical;
four auxiliary components are not four positive photon states.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put
$\omega(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here
$\omega$ is the temporal wave number, not the SI angular frequency; the
corresponding SI angular frequency is $c\omega$. Energy and momentum are
$E=\hbar c\omega$ in joules and $\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

The natural action is $S/\hbar$. Its canonical density in four dimensions has
unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$; the corresponding physical energy density is
$\hbar c$ times that density and has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
write $\phi_{\rm n}$ for a scalar field with length degree $-1$ and
$\psi_{\rm n}$ for a Dirac field with length degree $-3/2$. These are the
dimensions fixed by the selected free kinetic terms, not exact scaling
dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous dimensions, when present, are
separate quantities. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

The Clifford convention is $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$,
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}$, so the effective Clifford metric is
$-\eta$. In a supplied free Dirac model the displayed equation is
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$. The phase and Clifford choices are
conventions; this item proves no Dirac representation or field equation.
Time evolution is written $U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$ when a selected model has
actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ and its unitary group; the
corresponding Heisenberg conjugation is $O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. No such
Hamiltonian or group is constructed here. Where a free-field module uses an
inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the repository's
first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction.
Smeared fields are not thereby bounded, symmetric, self-adjoint, or
self-adjointly closable. Locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior are likewise supplied only by the
relevant constructed model modules. Test-function units can be chosen so a
specified smeared observable is dimensionless; there is no universal test
function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

Assume Countable Choice. On the future null cone write $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$, $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, $\mathbf k\ne0$, and use the measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. The fiber $p^\perp/\mathbb Cp$ has the positive quotient form of [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]. For each proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$, the action
$$[s(p)]\longmapsto[\Lambda s(\Lambda^{-1}p)]$$
is a unitary representation on the square-integrable quotient sections. It is strongly continuous. Under the unitary identification with $\mathcal H_T$ given by
$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Its bosonic Fock lift has joint spectrum the closed future cone
$$\overline V_+=\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\},$$
with the vacuum at $(0,\mathbf0)$. The energy is the nonnegative sector multiplier $\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ with the exact maximal square-integrability domain on each sector and square-summability over sectors. These are mathematical free-field representation statements.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

derivations.claim:
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, $|\mathbf n|^2=1$, so
$P_T^*=P_T$ and
$P_T^2=(I-\mathbf n\mathbf n^{\mathsf T})^2
=I-2\mathbf n\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}
+\mathbf n(\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}\mathbf n)\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}
=P_T$. Its kernel is $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf n\}$, so its range is
the two-dimensional plane $\mathbf n^\perp$. As a measurable bounded
orthogonal projection, its multiplication operator is idempotent on
$L^2$. If $P_Tu_r\to u$ with $P_Tu_r=u_r$, boundedness gives
$P_Tu=\lim_rP_Tu_r=\lim_ru_r=u$; hence the range is closed. A change at
$\mathbf k=0$ changes no $L^2$ vector because that singleton has Lebesgue
measure zero. This gives a positive rank-two transverse fiber almost
everywhere without selecting a polarization frame.

By [L1], each $\epsilon\in\mathcal K_0$ maps to a transverse vector
$T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-\mathbf n\epsilon^0$, and
$[\epsilon,\epsilon]_\eta=\|T\epsilon\|_{\mathcal H_T}^2\ge0$.
The kernel is exactly $\mathcal N$, so the induced norm is positive on
nonzero quotient classes. The supplier proves that $T$ is onto and that the
quotient is isometric to the complete Hilbert space $\mathcal H_T$; therefore
no negative-norm auxiliary direction becomes a physical state in this
quotient. This conclusion is conditional on the current draft interface.

The free Fock construction is understood under Countable Choice [A2].
By [F3], the unscaled multiplier $d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$ is
self-adjoint on its exact maximal sector-sum domain. The physical energy
operator in the selected model is $H_\gamma=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$,
so it has the same domain. In sector $n$ it is multiplication by
$H_n=\hbar c\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$. Every summand is nonnegative and
$\hbar c>0$ by [F2], so $H_n\ge0$; on the vacuum sector the empty sum is
zero. The strongly continuous unitary Lorentz action follows from [L2].
These are properties of the selected free model and do not assert an
interacting theory.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 assigns the empty zero-particle sum to the vacuum energy zero.
step 1.1 treats the zero momentum point as Lebesgue-null; step 2.1 treats the zero-particle sector.
step 1.1 proves rank two on every nonzero momentum fiber, including the one-photon sector.
step 1.1 proves the transverse rank is exactly two for every nonzero momentum.
step 1.1 assigns no effect to the massless cone apex because it is a measure-zero point.
step 2.1 carries Countable Choice [A2]; step 1.1 selects no global polarization frame.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

Assume Countable Choice. Work in the fixed length coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf w$; write $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$. For subsets $S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, say they are **spacelike separated** when $\eta(x-y,x-y)=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2-(x^0-y^0)^2>0$ for every $x\in S$ and $y\in T$. Let $A_0=0$ and let $A_i$ be the transverse potential operator-valued distribution of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]]. Set
$$F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,\qquad E_i=-\partial_0A_i,\qquad B_i=\epsilon_{irs}\partial_rA_s,$$
where $\epsilon_{irs}$ is the totally antisymmetric symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$. In the commutator formulas below, $\Delta=\sum_{r=1}^3\partial_r^2$ is the spatial Laplacian acting on $x-y$.
For a real antisymmetric test tensor $h=(h^{ab})$ with $h^{ab}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)$ and $h^{ab}=-h^{ba}$, define
$$F(h)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}F_{ab}(x)h^{ab}(x)\,d^4x =-A_b(\partial_a h^{ab}).$$
The effective test is conserved, $\partial_b\partial_a h^{ab}=0$, and $F(h)$ is unchanged by $A_b\mapsto A_b+\partial_b\lambda$ for smooth $\lambda$. Its one-particle coefficient $g_h$ is the vector $g_j$ of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]] for $j_i=-\partial_a h^{ai}$, so $F(h)=a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h)$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

Let $C_0=-i\Delta_0$, where $\Delta_0$ is the massless scalar causal commutator of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. As distributions in $x-y$,
$$[E_i(x),E_j(y)]=[B_i(x),B_j(y)] =(-\delta_{ij}\Delta+\partial_i\partial_j)C_0(x-y),$$
$$[E_i(x),B_j(y)]=\epsilon_{jri}\partial_0\partial_rC_0(x-y).$$
Every right-hand side has support in the closed causal cone. Hence compactly supported tests whose supports are spacelike separated in the stated Minkowski sense give commuting field-strength operators on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The quotient representation of [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]] makes these smeared field strengths Lorentz covariant: their on-shell coefficient depends on a polarization class only through $p_a\epsilon_b-p_b\epsilon_a$. These conclusions concern gauge-invariant free observables and do not assert locality of the Coulomb potential.

Assume Countable Choice and use the Minkowski coordinates and separation condition of [[lem-qft-photon-local-field-strength]], so $\eta(x-y,x-y)=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2-(x^0-y^0)^2$. A spacetime region $O$ means an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$ in its standard topology. A real antisymmetric test $h=(h^{ab})$ is supported in $O$ when each component $h^{ab}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R)$ has support contained in $O$. Two open regions $O_1,O_2$ are spacelike separated when $\eta(x-y,x-y)>0$ for every $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$. Let $g_h\in\mathcal H_T$ be the one-particle vector for such a test from [[lem-qft-photon-local-field-strength]]. The space $\mathcal H_T$ is separable: it is the range of the bounded projection $P_T$ on the separable space $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. Define
$$W_O(h)=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2\,g_h),$$
where $W_{\rm Segal}$ is the Weyl unitary of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. It is bounded and unitary, and its one-parameter group has the self-adjoint field-strength closure as generator. For every open region $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, let $\mathcal A(O)$ be the norm-closed unital $*$-algebra generated by $W_O(h)$ for real antisymmetric tests supported in $O$; equivalently its bounded real and imaginary parts are included as observables. If $O_1,O_2$ are spacelike separated by the stated Minkowski condition, then $\mathcal A(O_1)$ and $\mathcal A(O_2)$ commute.

derivations.claim:
The current operator construction is conditional on Countable Choice
[A2]. The test $h$ is real, smooth, compactly supported, and antisymmetric,
so it is an admissible input to [F1]. That carrier constructs
$F(h)=\frac12\int F_{ab}h^{ab}=-A_b(\partial_a h^{ab})$ as a smearing on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ and supplies its one-particle vector $g_h$.
Consequently the present $f(h)$ is exactly that free-model smearing under the
stated natural-normalization identification; it does not assign an operator
to $f_{ab}(x)$ at a point. Gauge invariance and covariance follow from the
same conditional carrier.

Suppose the compact supports of $h$ and $\ell$ are spacelike separated.
Their difference set is compact and disjoint from the closed causal cone,
so it has positive Euclidean distance from that closed set. Choose bounded small
open neighborhoods $O_h,O_\ell$ of the two supports whose difference set
remains outside the cone. By [F1], the smeared field-strength commutator
vanishes on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. By [L1],
$W_h\in\mathcal A(O_h)$ and $W_\ell\in\mathcal A(O_\ell)$, and these
local algebras commute. Their adjoints and linear combinations belong to
the same respective algebras; therefore the real and imaginary Hermitian
parts of $W_h,W_\ell$ commute. This is a conditional deduction in the
selected free model, not an observed outcome.

By [L1], $W_h$ is unitary, so $\|W_h\|=1$. The operators
$(W_h+W_h^*)/2$ and $(W_h-W_h^*)/(2i)$ are self-adjoint, and the triangle
inequality gives each norm at most one. They are therefore bounded local
Hermitian observables in the adopted model.

citations.quote:
Adopt a smooth local classical Maxwell–Dirac model on an open region of the
flat spacetime specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Let $A_{{\rm SI},a}$
be a supplied real $C^\infty$ electromagnetic covector potential and let
$\psi:\!U\to\mathbb C^4$ be a $C^\infty$ commuting spinor field. The charge
$q_{\rm SI}$ and rest mass $m_{\rm SI}>0$ are model inputs; for the electron
take $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$. Use the component, metric, Clifford, charge,
field-normalization, and unit conventions of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], [[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]],
[[def-qft-framework-units]], and the electromagnetic suppliers of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. In particular,
$D_a=\partial_a-iq_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar
=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a$ and $\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Adopt the local action density in natural normalization

$$\mathcal L_{\rm nat} =-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab} +\frac{i}{2}\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi -(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)-\mu\bar\psi\psi,$$

where $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_ba_a$ on the region where the
potential is supplied, $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$, and
$D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iq_{\rm n}a_a\bar\psi$. The physical action
is $S_{\rm cl}=\hbar\int_U\mathcal L_{\rm nat}\,d^4x$ with $x^0=ct$. For
compactly supported local variations this is the adopted classical
Maxwell–Dirac formulation; its Euler–Lagrange consequences are not postulated
as a proof in this item.

For a smooth gauge function $\chi$ in webers, the adopted local
transformation is
$A_{{\rm SI},a}\mapsto A_{{\rm SI},a}+\partial_a\chi$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{iq_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar}\psi$. It leaves $F=dA$ invariant and
makes $D_a\psi$ transform by the same phase. This is the covector form of the
SI potential rule in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. Gauge functions in the
local variation argument are compactly supported; no assertion is made about
large gauge transformations, nontrivial bundles, boundary charges, or
asymptotic sectors.

The model adopts the separately specified free Dirac representation of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]] and the positive free photon representation of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]] as the free-field correspondence used to
describe the selected species. This extra correspondence does not quantize
the interacting classical action. In particular, this postulate supplies no
interacting continuum four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, no globally
well-posed coupled PDE, no pointwise operator-valued composite current, no
scattering or LSZ construction, and no regulator-removal or
nonperturbative-existence result.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the oriented, time-oriented Minkowski model, length coordinates, metric,
and SI/natural dictionary of [[def-qft-framework-units]], with
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $x^0=ct$. Use the gamma matrices,
Dirac adjoint, and effective Clifford metric of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]: $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$,
and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$. Assume Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]] for the mathematical QFT gauge-data supplier; the
unit conversions below do not themselves spend a choice principle.

Identify the SI charge and mass symbols $q,m$ in
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]] with $q_{\rm SI},m_{\rm SI}$ here. Its natural
coupling $g$ is $q_{\rm n}$ below, and its inverse-length mass $\mu$ is the
same $m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Let $q_{\rm SI}\in\mathbb R$ be a selected charge parameter in coulombs and
$m_{\rm SI}>0$ a selected rest-mass parameter in kilograms. They are inputs
of the chosen model; neither is derived from Maxwell's equations. Set
$\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and
$q_{\rm n}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$, which is dimensionless under the
framework units of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. For an electron use
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ and
$e_{\rm n}=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}>0$, so $q_{\rm n}=-e_{\rm n}$.
Use $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the measured current-SI
$\mu_0$ of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. These definitions therefore do not
assign an exact numerical value to $q_{\rm n}$, $e_{\rm n}$, or
$\varepsilon_0$.

In a named inertial chart, let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ be the
electromagnetic potential when one is supplied, with components in
$\mathrm{T\,m}$ under [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. Define the canonical potential and
field-strength components by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have engineering dimensions $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm m^{-2}$,
respectively. With the metric-lowered potential
$A_{{\rm SI},a}=\eta_{ab}A^b_{\rm SI}$, the potential component convention is
$A_{{\rm SI},0}=-\varphi/c$ and $A_{{\rm SI},i}=A_i$. The covariant derivative
in the selected QED model is

$$D_a:=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a =\partial_a-\frac{iq_{\rm SI}}{\hbar}A_{{\rm SI},a},$$

since $q_{\rm n}a_a=q_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar$. Both terms in $D_a$
have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. If the SI gauge function $\chi$ has unit
$\mathrm{Wb}=\mathrm{T\,m^2}$, then $q_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar$ is dimensionless;
the corresponding natural gauge function
$\lambda=\chi/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ is dimensionless and
$q_{\rm n}\lambda=q_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar$. These conversions apply to smooth
local gauge transformations; they assert no boundary condition, asymptotic
charge sector, or global gauge-fixing result.

If a separately specified finite regulator introduces Hamiltonian
eigenvalues, they have unit joule; this definition introduces no regulator.
The field components and units refer to the selected inertial chart, not to a
new observer congruence or a cross-framework identification.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]]. No field equation is required to define the vocabulary; the existence theorem recalled in (a) has the additional hypotheses stated there.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. When $\Omega$ is open and star-shaped, $I$ is an interval with at least two elements, and the jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, satisfy $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ in the stated restriction convention, and smooth potentials for smooth data satisfying the same equations; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put
$\omega(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here
$\omega$ is the temporal wave number, not the SI angular frequency; the
corresponding SI angular frequency is $c\omega$. Energy and momentum are
$E=\hbar c\omega$ in joules and $\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

The natural action is $S/\hbar$. Its canonical density in four dimensions has
unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$; the corresponding physical energy density is
$\hbar c$ times that density and has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
write $\phi_{\rm n}$ for a scalar field with length degree $-1$ and
$\psi_{\rm n}$ for a Dirac field with length degree $-3/2$. These are the
dimensions fixed by the selected free kinetic terms, not exact scaling
dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous dimensions, when present, are
separate quantities. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

The Clifford convention is $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$,
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}$, so the effective Clifford metric is
$-\eta$. In a supplied free Dirac model the displayed equation is
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$. The phase and Clifford choices are
conventions; this item proves no Dirac representation or field equation.
Time evolution is written $U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$ when a selected model has
actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ and its unitary group; the
corresponding Heisenberg conjugation is $O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. No such
Hamiltonian or group is constructed here. Where a free-field module uses an
inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the repository's
first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction.
Smeared fields are not thereby bounded, symmetric, self-adjoint, or
self-adjointly closable. Locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior are likewise supplied only by the
relevant constructed model modules. Test-function units can be chosen so a
specified smeared observable is dimensionless; there is no universal test
function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

Assume Countable Choice and use the conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open, let each $a_a:U\to\mathbb R$
be a smooth real potential component, and let $\psi:U\to\mathbb C^4$
be a smooth commuting spinor. The real gauge parameter is a smooth
$\alpha:U\to\mathbb R$, and all fields, derivatives and compactly supported
smooth variations below are on this same $U$ (including $U=\mathbb R^4$). Use the symmetrized classical density
$$\mathcal L_D=\frac i2\{\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi-(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\}-\mu\bar\psi\psi,\qquad D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+ig a_a\bar\psi.$$
For compactly supported smooth variations, its spinor Euler equation is $(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi=0$ and its adjoint. The density is invariant under the gauge transformation in [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. On solutions,
$$\partial_a j^a=0,\qquad j^a=g\bar\psi\gamma^a\psi.$$
In SI variables the corresponding Hamiltonian density has the sign convention
$$\psi^\dagger\!\left[c\,\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot(-i\hbar\nabla-q\mathbf A)+\beta mc^2+q\phi\right]\psi.$$
These are conditional variational identities for smooth commuting classical fields. They assert no global existence theorem for the coupled field equations, no quantum current product, and no empirical measurement.

derivations.claim:
The action uses length coordinates $x^0=ct$ by [F8]. Put
$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$,
$a_a=A_{{\rm SI},a}/S_0$, and
$g=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$. Then
$ga_a=q_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar$ by [F1], so the matter covariant
derivative in [A1] is exactly $D_a=\partial_a-iga_a$ in [L1]. For an SI
gauge function $\chi$, put $\alpha=\chi/S_0$; then
$g\alpha=q_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar$. Thus the SI transformation of [A1]
becomes $a_a\mapsto a_a+\partial_a\alpha$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{ig\alpha}\psi$. Differentiating the phase shows
$D'_a\psi'=e^{ig\alpha}D_a\psi$; commuting smooth partial derivatives
give $F'=F$.

Countable Choice [A2] is carried for the separately adopted free-field
correspondence; the classical local variation below itself requires no
choice operation. Let $R_D=(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$. The compact-support first-variation
identity in [L1] is local: for every $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4)$,
integration by parts in the symmetrized density gives
$$\frac{\delta S_D}{\hbar} =2\operatorname{Re}\int_U\zeta^\dagger\beta R_D\,d^4x.$$
Indeed, the derivative terms use
$\int_U\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\zeta=-\int_U(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\zeta$
and
$-\int_U(D_a\bar\zeta)\gamma^a\psi=\int_U\bar\zeta\gamma^aD_a\psi$;
there are no boundary terms because $\zeta$ is compactly supported. If
$R_D(x_0)\ne0$, continuity gives a ball $B\subset U$ on which $R_D$ is
nonzero. Choose $\rho$ from [F6] supported in $B$ and positive on a smaller
ball, and set $\zeta=\rho\beta R_D$. By [F5],
$\zeta^\dagger\beta R_D=\rho|R_D|^2$, so the first variation is
$2\int_U\rho|R_D|^2d^4x>0$, contradicting stationarity. Therefore
$R_D=0$ on $U$, and taking its adjoint gives the adjoint Dirac equation.
This is a local consequence of compact variations, not an existence claim.

Multiplying the Dirac equation by $\bar\psi$ gives
$i\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi=\mu\bar\psi\psi$; multiplying its
adjoint by $\psi$ gives
$-i(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi=\mu\bar\psi\psi$. Subtracting the
equations gives
$(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi+\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi=0$.
Expanding $D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iga_a\bar\psi$ and
$D_a\psi=\partial_a\psi-iga_a\psi$ cancels the two gauge-potential
terms, leaving $\partial_a(\bar\psi\gamma^a\psi)=0$. The natural
current in [L1] is $j_{\rm n}^a=g\bar\psi\gamma^a\psi$. By step 1.1,
$S_0g=\mu_0q_{\rm SI}c$, so the SI current associated to
$\partial_aF_{\rm SI}^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$ is
$j^a=(S_0/\mu_0)j_{\rm n}^a=q_{\rm SI}c\bar\psi\gamma^a\psi$ and is
conserved because the conversion factor is constant. Using [F5],
$j^0=q_{\rm SI}c\psi^\dagger\psi$ and
$j^i=q_{\rm SI}c\psi^\dagger\alpha_i\psi$, hence
$j=(c\rho_q,\mathbf J_q)$ with the displayed SI charge and current
densities.

Write the natural action density from [A1] as
$-\frac14f_{ab}f^{ab}+\mathcal L_D$. For a real compactly supported
variation $\delta a_b$, antisymmetry of $f^{ab}$ gives
$$\delta(-\tfrac14f_{ab}f^{ab})=-f^{ab}\partial_a\delta a_b.$$
The matter variation is
$$\delta\mathcal L_D =\frac i2\left[\bar\psi\gamma^b(-ig\delta a_b)\psi -(ig\delta a_b\bar\psi)\gamma^b\psi\right] =g\bar\psi\gamma^b\psi\,\delta a_b.$$
Integrating the Maxwell term by parts and using compact support therefore
gives
$$\frac{\delta S}{\hbar} =\int_U(\partial_af^{ab}+g\bar\psi\gamma^b\psi)\delta a_b\,d^4x.$$
By [F5], $\bar\psi\gamma^0\psi=\psi^\dagger\psi$ and
$\bar\psi\gamma^i\psi=\psi^\dagger\alpha_i\psi$ are real. If a component
$G^b=\partial_af^{ab}+g\bar\psi\gamma^b\psi$ were nonzero at a point,
continuity would give a ball in $U$ on which it has fixed nonzero sign.
Choose a nonnegative bump $\rho$ there using [F6] and vary only $a_b$ by
$\delta a_b=\rho$. The displayed variation would then be nonzero, contrary
to stationarity. Thus every $G^b$ vanishes pointwise and
$\partial_af^{ab}=-g\bar\psi\gamma^b\psi$. Since
$F_{\rm SI}^{ab}=S_0f^{ab}$ and
$S_0g=\mu_0q_{\rm SI}c$, this is exactly
$\partial_aF_{\rm SI}^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$. For $b=0$, [F2] gives
$\partial_aF^{a0}=-\operatorname{div}E/c$, so the source equation becomes
$\operatorname{div}E=\mu_0c^2\rho_q=\rho_q/\varepsilon_0$ by [F3].
For $b=i$, [F2] gives
$\partial_aF^{ai}=c^{-2}\partial_tE_i-(\operatorname{curl}B)_i$,
which yields $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0\mathbf J_q+c^{-2}\partial_tE$.
Finally, $F=dA$ and commuting partial derivatives give
$\partial_{[a}F_{bc]}=0$, whose spatial components are
$\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$. These are
the smooth equations in [F4], derived conditionally from the adopted action;
they are not evidence that the model describes nature.

citations.quote:
For a formal indeterminate $z$, let $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ be the commutative ring of sequences $(a_0,a_1,\ldots)$ written $\sum_{n\ge0}a_nz^n$, with coefficientwise addition and Cauchy-product multiplication. No convergence of a numerical series is part of this definition. For $d\ge1$, matrices over $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ use the usual finite matrix addition and multiplication.

Use the finite graph phase data of [[def-qft-qed-finite-graph-gauge-data]] and the QED $U(1)$, Clifford, and natural-unit conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. Let $K_0(\zeta)\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$ be an invertible base matrix and let $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be its finite link-hopping matrix. The admissible covariant families satisfy
$$ K_0(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta K_0(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1},\qquad V(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta V(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}. $$
The scalar base $K_0=mI_d$, $m\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, is an explicit admissible case. Define
$$ K(z;\zeta):=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta),\qquad S(z;\zeta):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-zK_0(\zeta)^{-1}V(\zeta))^nK_0(\zeta)^{-1}. $$
The coefficient of each power $z^n$ in $S$ is one finite matrix. The item defines this formal candidate; the following lemma proves its two-sided inverse and covariance properties. Define $\det A$ for a finite matrix $A$ over $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ by the Leibniz formula $\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{j=1}^d A_{j,\sigma(j)}$.

For a real vertex phase $\theta=(\theta_x)_{x\in X}\in\mathbb R^X$, define
$$
\zeta_e^\theta:=e^{i(\theta_{s(e)}-\theta_{t(e)})}\zeta_e,\qquad
D_\theta:=\operatorname{diag}_{x\in X}(e^{i\theta_x}I_r)\in GL_d(\mathbb C).
$$
Define the link-hopping matrix $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ by its $x,y$ block indexed by $x,y\in X$
$$
V(\zeta)_{xy}:=\sum_{\substack{e\in E\\s(e)=x,\ t(e)=y}}T_e\zeta_e .
$$
An empty sum is the zero $r\times r$ matrix. Additional fixed diagonal blocks belong to a separate base matrix. These data are finite-dimensional algebraic data; the phases are external parameters, not rotor multiplication operators on $L^2(\mathbb T^E)$.

Use the fixed Minkowski coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)=(ct,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, on an open coordinate domain $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with its standard topology. Each $x^a$ has unit metre. For a smooth scalar component $u:U\to\mathbb R$ or $u:U\to\mathbb C$, define $\partial_a u:=\partial u/\partial x^a$; thus $\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t$ at fixed $\mathbf x$, $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x^j$ for $j=1,2,3$, and each $\partial_a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Raise derivative indices with $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$. The fields in this definition are smooth maps
$$\phi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathbf A\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R^3),\qquad \psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4),\qquad \chi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R).$$
Define the lower-potential component maps $A_a:U\to\mathbb R$ by $A_0=-\phi/c$ and $A_j=\mathbf A_j$; collectively $(A_a)$ is the real covector potential in this chart. Then $F_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ has smooth real component maps $F_{ab}:U\to\mathbb R$. The spinor is an ordinary commuting $\mathbb C^4$-valued map, not a tuple of Grassmann generators. Its Dirac adjoint is the smooth row-valued map $\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta:U\to(\mathbb C^4)^*$, using the fixed matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], so $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$. In fixed SI units, $\phi$ is in volts, each $A_a$ is in $\mathrm{T\,m}$, $\psi$ is assigned field dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$, and $\chi$ is in webers; these unit labels accompany the maps and do not identify $q$ with a measured charge. For periodic spatial domains, the same component and unit conventions apply to smooth periodic coordinate lifts, with the quotient domain specified by the item using them.

For the SI-normalization bookkeeping, let $c>0$ (m s$^{-1}$), $\hbar>0$ (J s), $\mu_0>0$ (N A$^{-2}$), a real charge parameter $q$ (C), and a mass parameter $m>0$ (kg) be symbolic inputs; put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. In the current SI, $c$ and $h$ are defining constants while $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined; the formula below keeps $\mu_0$ symbolic and assigns it no numerical value. Use the lower-potential convention
$$A_a=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A),$$
where $A_a$ has units T m, $\phi$ is in volts, and $\mathbf A$ is in T m. Define
$$S_0=\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c},\qquad a_a=A_a/S_0,\qquad f_{ab}=\partial_aa_b-\partial_ba_a,$$
$$\mu=mc/\hbar,\qquad g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}=q/\sqrt{\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad D_a=\partial_a-ig a_a.$$
Here $D_a$ acts on $\psi\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C^4)$ by $(D_a\psi)(x)=\partial_a\psi(x)-ig a_a(x)\psi(x)$, again a smooth map $U\to\mathbb C^4$. Thus $a_a$ and $\mu$ have units m$^{-1}$, $f_{ab}$ has units m$^{-2}$, and $g$ is dimensionless. For $\psi$ with units m$^{-3/2}$, both $-\tfrac14 f_{ab}f^{ab}$ and $\bar\psi(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$ have units m$^{-4}$; their integral over $d^4x$ is dimensionless and represents the action divided by $\hbar$ in this normalization.

For the real smooth gauge-parameter map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R$ in webers, put $\alpha:=\chi/S_0\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ (dimensionless) and use
$$A'_a=A_a+\partial_a\chi,\qquad a'_a=a_a+\partial_a\alpha,\qquad \psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi.$$
The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

derivations.claim: Put $B:=K_0^{-1}V$. The coefficient of $z^n$ in $S$ is $(-B)^nK_0^{-1}$, a finite matrix, so the series defines an element of $M_d(\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket)$ without an analytic convergence assumption.

Each link block transforms as $T_e\zeta_e^\theta=e^{i\theta_{s(e)}}(T_e\zeta_e)e^{-i\theta_{t(e)}}$; summing links in each block gives $V(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta V(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}$. With [A1], the assumed covariance of $K_0$ gives the same conjugation for each coefficient of $K$; [F3] supplies the separate continuum phase convention, without identifying graph vertices with spacetime points.

Since $K=K_0(I+zB)$, multiplication gives $KS=K_0(I+zB)\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^nK_0^{-1}$. In the product $(I+zB)\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n$, the constant coefficient is $I$ and the two contributions to every positive-degree coefficient cancel; hence $KS=I$.
Also $K_0^{-1}K=I+zB$, so $SK=\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n(I+zB)=I$ by the same coefficientwise cancellation. Thus $S$ is the two-sided formal inverse.
Substituting the conjugated $K_0,V$ into the defining series for $S$ conjugates each finite coefficient by $D_\theta$, proving $S(z;\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta S(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}$.

Use the path $\zeta_s=\zeta^{s\theta}$, $D_s=D_{s\theta}$ and the definitions of $K_s,S_s,\delta$ in the Statement. Differentiate $K_sS_s=I$ coefficientwise at $s=0$. This gives $(\delta K)S+K(\delta S)=0$, hence $\delta S=-S(\delta K)S$ using $K^{-1}=S$.
From $D_s=e^{is\Theta}$, direct differentiation gives $\delta K=i[\Theta,K]$. Therefore $-S\,i[\Theta,K]\,S=-iS\Theta KS+iSK\Theta S=-iS\Theta+i\Theta S=i[\Theta,S]$.

For ordinary invertible finite matrices $A,B$, expand the product:
$B^{-1}(B-A)A^{-1}=B^{-1}BA^{-1}-B^{-1}AA^{-1}=A^{-1}-B^{-1}$.
This is exactly the resolvent identity in the Statement.

At z=0, S(0)=K0^{-1}; steps 1.1–2.2 include the constant coefficient.
